title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, the E155 Microprocessor PCB was soldered with the UPduino v3.1 FPGA, an STM Nucleo-L432KC MCU board, and various switches, SMT resistors, LEDS, and other electronic components. A design was implemented on the FPGA to demonstrate the functionality of the on-board high-speed oscillator by blinking one of the on-board LEDs, a simple XOR and AND combinational logic to light up two other on-board LEDs, and logic control signal from a 4 bit representation DIP switch to toggle an off-board seven segment LED to represent a single hexademical digit. The high speed oscillator was configured at a frequency of 24 MHz and divided down using a counter to achieve a blinking frequency of ~2.4 Hz.

title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, the E155 Microprocessor PCB was soldered with the UPduino v3.1 FPGA, an STM Nucleo-L432KC MCU board, and various switches, SMT resistors, LEDS, and other electronic components. A design was implemented on the FPGA to demonstrate the functionality of the on-board high-speed oscillator by blinking one of the on-board LEDs, a simple XOR and AND combinational logic to light up two other on-board LEDs, and logic control signal from a 4 bit representation DIP switch to toggle an off-board seven segment LED to represent a single hexademical digit. The high speed oscillator was configured at a frequency of 24 MHz and divided down using a counter to achieve a blinking frequency of ~2.4 Hz.

title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 24 MHz. Then, a counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down so that the blinking frequency could be easily visualized using one of the on-board LEDs. Counter is a variable with a width of 24 bits. Therefore when selecting the bit to represent the LED we can set the 2.4Hz blinking LED to be the most significant 24th bit as this will be on. The \[\text{target frequency = input frequency / division factor} \] Therefore as the target frequency is 2.4Hz and the input frequency is 24MHz, we require the division factor to close to 10,000,000. We can roughly achieve this by selecting the 24th bit to be a 1 because \[2^{23} = 8,388,608 \implies \text{target frequency} = \frac{2.4MHz}{8,388,608} \approx 2.4Hz\]
The DIP switch was used to drive an XOR and AND function to light two other LEDs by assigning two sets of to different bits which were encoding in the DIP switch. A testbench with the 4 different outcomes for each output was created.
As for the seven segment LED, it has seven individual LEDs which each need to be driven by a +3.3V common anode – produced by the FPGA – and connected to a pin on the FPGA. Similarly a testbench with all 16 single digit hexadecimal representation outputs was run.
I use the industry standard Radiant Software to set up my SystemVerilog files to write the hardware for the FPGA and complete pin assignment to the 3 on-board LEDs and off-board seven segment LEDs. Once the files synthesized, a .bin file was created in my project folder directory.
Next I used the openFPGA to upload my program to the FPGA. In my local terminal, I input the commandline openFPGALoader -b ice40_generic -c ft232  -f </path/to/bin_filename.bin> to program my FPGA. For this project, I also had to short my UPduino and +5V in located on J3 of the PCB in order to provide power to the board.

text:

Figure 2 shows the physical layout of the design. An internal 100 kΩ pullup resistor was used to ensure the active low reset pin was not floating for the LEDs. The each output LED connecting to the seven segment was connected using a 220 Ω current-limiting resistor to ensure the output current
\[I = \frac{3.3V}{220Ω} = 15mA \]
did not exceed the maximum output current of the FPGA I/O RBG pins which is 24mA.

title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Results and Discussion
The design most of the intended design objectives. Figure 3 shows a screenshot of the seven segment LED showing an 8 when the bit representation 00001000 is triggered on the DIP switch.






NoteFigure 3: Seven segment LED








Figure 3: Seven segment LED displaying 8 as hexademical representation when the DIP switch is turned on





If a more precise output frequency was desired, a more sophisticated counter could be developed. The current frequency of oscillation is actually closer to 2.8Hz rather than the 2.4Hz desired. The current design only allows for the clock to be divided by powers of two. Testing the reset button on the hardware also demonstrates that it functions as the LED does not blink when my assigned reset switch is pressed.

Testbench Simulation
The design met the specifications for the seven segment, the counter, and the on-board LED logic.






NoteFigure 4: QuestSim Simulation








Figure 4: QuestSim simulation square wave form











NoteFigure 5: Testbench








Figure 5: QuestSim simulation showing the internal signals and passing LED test cases for the one line assign statements and the seven segment as well as the cases for the counter and enable functionality





A few shortcomings of this project are not including the test cases for the counter reaching its max value and verification of internal signals for the top module. Other excellent specifications could be met such as verifying the reset, enable, and other top module behaviour such as the HSOSC and the connections. These I did not have enough time to work on given the many logisitical challenges I had with this project.

title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Conclusion
The design successfully produces SystemVerilog files and project synthesis to verify logic controls to two LEDs, a blinking LED with a clock divider, and a seven segment LED to represent the hexadecimal representation of 8 bit signal from a DIP switch. In total I spent 65 hours on this lab in one week.

title: Lab 1: FPGA, MCU Setup and Testing
text:
AI Prototype Summary
For this lab, students were tasked to see if “can my LLMs of choice generate SystemVerilog that compiles, synthesizes and exhibits correct behavior?” We were told to prompt our favorite LLM
“Write SystemVerilog HDL to leverage the internal high speed oscillator in the Lattice UP5K FPGA and blink an LED at 2 Hz. Take full advantage of SystemVerilog syntax, for example, using logic instead of wire and reg.”
Figures 6 and 7 demonstrate the output when the SystemVerilog code was synthesized.






NoteFigure 6: LLM’s first file compilation attempt








Figure 6: Radiant Software demonstrates that the files did not compile and fails











NoteFigure 7: Recomplation for correction








Figure 7: Recomplication after the LLM was prompted to correct itself. SystemVerilog code included. Still led to a failed simulation





From the code generation, I conclude that the output is not the most accurate. There are newly constructed syntax such as this localparan int unsigned which I have never come across before. During the first synthesis, the errors were that the code generated was trying to use a module that did not exist the first time around or was not include. In the next iteration, the module was able to be instantiated.
With these results, I would not trust Claude LLM to generate me code but perhaps would use it to spot errors in my code or file hierachy.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text: In this lab, I used the MCU to play music by using two timers on the board namely the TIM6 and TIM16 to generate square square waves. These square waves were toggles at specific frequency for defined durations. The music provided in this lab is given in the form of a list of tuples where the first element of the tuple is the frequency of the note and the second element is the duration in milliseconds. The provided sequence of tuples results in the tune Fur Elise by Beethoven.

text: In this lab, I used the MCU to play music by using two timers on the board namely the TIM6 and TIM16 to generate square square waves. These square waves were toggles at specific frequency for defined durations. The music provided in this lab is given in the form of a list of tuples where the first element of the tuple is the frequency of the note and the second element is the duration in milliseconds. The provided sequence of tuples results in the tune Fur Elise by Beethoven.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
When designing this system, I used the example blink file to view how existing drivers flash to the PB3 GPIO pin. Once the basic setup with the blinking LED was completed, I followed the style of how drivers were coded for timers and coded drivers for TIM6 and TIM16. This means that I wrote header files for the TIM6 and TIM16 registers. I determined that I would use TIM6 to control the frequency of the toggle rate – which sets the frequency of the note and I would use the TIM16 to control the duration of the note. When instantiating TIM6 and TIM16, I intially set both their prescale values to 0 and their auto-reload registers 0xFFFF the maximum value. My plan was to configure these fields to provide the specified frequency and duration when I used them in their functions. In the setup, I also had to enable both timers and the GPIOA pin for PA6 to have toggle functionality. The GPIOA PA6 pin was connected to an 8-ohm speaker using an LM386 audio amplifier with a gain of 200.
To play the music I wrote a while loop iterating through each tuple in the music.
Below are my calculations to show the minimum and maximum duration supported, the minimum and maximum frequency supported, and calculations which show that all the notes in Fur Elise can be replicated to within 1% accuracy.






NoteFigure 1: Minimum and maximum calculations for the frequency and duration supported








Figure 1: Explanation of min/max frequency and duration











NoteFigure 2: Sheet with exhaustive calculation of percentage error of all notes in Fur Elise.








Figure 2: Sheet with exhaustive calculation of percentage error of all notes in Fur Elise. The maximum error for a note is 0.03% which is well below the 1% error tolerance level

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Conclusion
I was able to successfully achieve the goals for this lab to play Fur Elise and a song of my own choice using the timers onboard the STM microcontroller. In total I spend 30 hours on this lab. Jumping and practice the skill of reading the block diagram and debugging which bits in which register to turn on was useful to help me know which sections to turn on and off. It was also valuable debugging how a counter can be set and reset to oscillate a signal in real time.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
AI Prototype Summary
For this lab, students were tasked to see if “What timers should I use on the STM32L432KC to generate frequencies ranging from 220Hz to 1kHz? What’s the best choice of timer if I want to easily connect it to a GPIO pin? What formulae are relevant, and what registers need to be set to configure them properly?” We were told to prompt our favorite LLM.
I used Claude AI and it suggests that TIM2 would be the best first for two main reasons. (1) The TIM2 is 32 bits wide as opposite to my choice of using the TIM16 and TIM6 which both are 16 bits wide. This means TIM2 has a higher resolution for the frequency of choice, however, this does not really matter because in software we are rounding the numbers for ARR regardless when you set it. (2) Claude also mentions that TIM2 is the simplest to use because it has no break/dead-time logic, so we don’t need to set up MOE – I’m not sure what does it but it doesn’t look like we set this up using TIM6 or TIM16 either. Claude also provided some example code to set up TIM2.
In summary, I think the Claude was a good starting point especially with the table to analyze the trade offs between each timer but I don’t think the advice should be followed verbatim. I draw on this conclusion based on the lack of relevant explanation for the set up MOE argument.
